issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'full sensory reliving' suggests highly vivid, poorly contextualized trauma memory, which sits in marked tension with 'I can talk about what happened very easily.' Those two can sometimes coexist, but as a three-item profile with shame on recall they pull in opposing directions and are clinically questionable together.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: 'Avoid enclosed spaces' is not clearly coherent with the rest of the profile for sexual assault as described here. The threat and memory items center on being followed, danger in unfamiliar places, delays, shame, and vivid reliving; enclosed spaces introduces a more specific situational avoidance that is not supported by the memory/threat content and looks disconnected from the formulation, especially since Triggers is not active in this case.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits in tension with 'When I remember the event I feel intense shame' and 'Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time.' Severe shame and terror on recall usually make disclosure difficult rather than easy, so this combination is clinically questionable within the same node.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant
issues.explanation: 'Ruminate about how to get even with assailant' is a poor fit with the rest of the profile for this trauma type and patient presentation. The Memory and Threat items emphasize shame, terror, hypervigilance, and avoidance, which is more consistent with fear-based post-assault PTSD; revenge-focused rumination pulls toward a different emotional/cognitive stance and lacks support elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: 'Gambling' is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly anchored to the rest of the presentation. The dominant active formulation is Memory↔Threat↔Maladaptive Strategies around trauma recollection and danger monitoring after sexual assault; gambling for excitement/distracting oneself is too nonspecific and does not connect clearly to the patient's other selected threat and memory items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Enclosed Spaces' appears to be a trigger/avoidance cue rather than a maladaptive strategy, and it is poorly matched to the rest of the profile. The threat and memory items center on being followed, danger in unfamiliar places, shame, terror, and speechless recall; avoidance of enclosed spaces is a different contextual pattern that is not otherwise supported here.

vignette: At fifty-three, David had spent the better part of two decades navigating the complex caseloads of a county social services office. His life shifted abruptly five years ago, during a walk home past a dimly lit municipal underpass. The attack was sudden and violent. He was forced into a narrow, windowless maintenance closet, the heavy door shutting with a final, metallic click that severed him from the world outside. He remembers the suffocating weight of the confined dark, the cold concrete against his back, and the terrifying suspension of time. He did not know how long he remained there, nor could he predict when the door would open. When the man finally released him and David stumbled into the alley, the ordinary streets around him felt irrevocably compromised. In the months that followed, David's internal landscape became a series of uncharted territories. When memories of the underpass surfaced, they did not arrive as organized accounts. He knew precisely what had transpired, yet the words consistently dissolved in his throat, leaving a hollow, inarticulate terror that rose in his chest with a force that stole his breath. Alongside that terror sat a heavy, hot shame that coated him long after the images faded. When the images returned, he also began pushing them out of his mind, gripping his steering wheel until his knuckles blanched, telling himself that if he simply refused to dwell on the past, the pressure would ease. But the space he tried to clear was never empty. It was occupied by a quiet, relentless rumination on revenge, a mental script he ran while folding his wife's laundry or waiting for the coffee maker to finish, turning over every imagined scenario where he finally made the assailant pay for what was taken from him. David's daily environment became a landscape of calibrated risks. As a social worker, his role required moving through unfamiliar neighborhoods and entering small, private offices to conduct intake assessments. He came to believe that unfamiliarity was synonymous with vulnerability. He began tracing the same three blocks to the clinic, memorizing sightlines and exits before stepping out of his car. In his own vehicle, he developed the habit of checking behind him before entering the building, his hand lingering on the door handle, scanning the street for shadows or unfamiliar vehicles. When a case file required a longer wait than anticipated, or a client was late to an appointment, his stomach tightened; he was certain that delays meant something bad had already begun. The clinic's windowless consultation room became untenable. The four walls felt like the maintenance closet returning. He began rescheduling clients to the bright, open staff lounge, explaining it was for better accessibility, though he knew it was because he needed to see the doors and the windows. Over time, these habits calcified into a rigid routine. He lost a supervisory position to a younger caseworker who willingly navigated new territory and sat quietly in closed offices. At home, his wife noticed he flinched when she approached him after he'd been staring out the window, his body rigid with the same terror he felt when the elevator hesitated between floors. He stopped suggesting new restaurants or routes, sticking only to places where the layout felt predictable. What finally brought David to my office was a Tuesday morning when he sat in his car for twenty minutes, unable to cross the bridge to the clinic because the morning traffic had stalled. He felt a profound exhaustion, a quiet realization that the man who attacked him five years ago still dictated his routines. He was hoping for a way to stop scanning the rearview mirror and to find words that did not taste like ash, but what frightened him most was the certainty that the fear had already become the only reliable thing he had left.
